## Why the review looks like this
The sixteen-bit floating point candidate is chosen for initial validation because it needs the least energy per inference and has the lowest latency even though it draws more power while running than the eight-bit integer builds. Success comparisons remain undecided because the confidence intervals for each candidate overlap the tolerance band and the current number of trials is too small to rule out a meaningful difference. The deliberately miscalibrated builds are stopped at the simple input check because that check detects the calibration error independently of the other audit scores. The AI judge’s record shows it is sensitive to wording, judges only the end state and produces more false alarms on novel objects, so it must be re‑validated before any reliance is placed on its output.

## Questions to resolve before deployment
- How many additional trials are needed to shrink the confidence interval around the success rate so that the upper bound stays within ten percentage points of the full-precision reference?
- Does the sixteen-bit floating point candidate keep its latency advantage when the device operates under sustained power limits?
- Can the simple input check be made robust enough to catch calibration drift across temperature variations without increasing false rejects on nominal units?
- What wording changes to the AI judge prompt reduce false alarms on unseen objects while preserving detection of genuine failures?
